sections.label: Passage 1
sections.title: The quiet power of boredom
sections.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–10.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Boredom has a poor reputation. It is the feeling we rush to extinguish with a phone, a snack or a quick scroll, as though it were a minor malfunction of the mind rather than a normal signal. Yet psychologists increasingly argue that boredom is not a problem to be solved but a prompt to be heeded. When nothing in our environment holds our attention, the mind begins to wander, and wandering is where a surprising amount of original thinking begins.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Researchers distinguish between two broad kinds of boredom. The milder, more open variety arrives when a task is easy or repetitive and the mind is left free to drift. The heavier variety, sometimes called reactive boredom, arrives with a sense of being trapped and restless, and it is the kind most likely to make people reach for distractions. The difference matters because the lighter form is linked to imagination, while the heavier form tends to produce irritability and withdrawal.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In one well-known study, participants who were made to copy numbers from a phone book for fifteen minutes later performed better on an unusual-use task than participants who had been entertained the whole time. The tedious copying seemed to loosen something in their thinking. The researchers suggested that a quiet, under-stimulated interval gives the brain room to make unusual connections that a busy schedule crowds out.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There is also a creative argument for protecting fallow time. Many writers and inventors describe their best ideas arriving not at the desk but in the shower, on a walk or while staring out of a train window. These moments share a common feature: the conscious mind is occupied with something gentle and automatic, leaving the rest of the mind to work below the surface. Boredom, in this sense, is the doorway to that deeper work.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Boredom may even help with motivation. When every idle moment is filled with polished, professional entertainment, people lose the gentle discomfort that pushes them to begin something of their own. A little boredom restores agency: it reminds us that we, not an algorithm, get to decide what to do next. The empty afternoon becomes an invitation rather than an emergency.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this is a case for deliberate misery. Prolonged, helpless boredom is a genuine risk, especially for people who are isolated or unemployed. The useful claim is narrower: brief, ordinary boredom is a healthy signal, and the habitual suppression of it may cost us more imagination than we realise. Leaving gaps in the day is not laziness; it is maintenance for a mind that is otherwise never allowed to rest.

sections.label: Passage 2
sections.title: Why cities are learning to sleep in the dark
sections.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 11–20.

passage.title: Why cities are learning to sleep in the dark

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of human history, night was dark by necessity. Then electric light arrived, and within a century the night sky over cities had been erased. Today a different idea is spreading: that darkness, too, is infrastructure worth protecting. A growing number of towns dim their lamps after midnight, not to save money alone but to recover something they did not know they had lost.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The argument rests on ecology. Artificial light at night disrupts the migration of birds, the hunting patterns of bats, and the reproduction of many insects. Street lighting tuned to the wrong spectrum can pull moths into a fatal orbit and break the food chains that depend on them. When a town dims itself, local surveys often record a quick return of nocturnal wildlife.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Human health is part of the case as well. Exposure to bright, blue-rich light in the late hours can delay the body's production of melatonin and disturb sleep. Several municipalities have begun replacing cool white lamps with warmer, lower outputs, and dimming them on a schedule that follows the natural fall of night rather than a fixed timetable.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Opponents worry about safety. The intuitive belief is that brighter streets are safer streets, yet the evidence is mixed. Some studies find little relationship between overall lighting levels and crime, while others find that targeted lighting at specific crossings and pathways helps more than blanket illumination. The question, then, is not simply how much light but where and when it falls.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Technology makes the compromise easier. Adaptive systems sense movement and brighten only the stretch of pavement in use, then fade again. Such systems cut energy use and light spill while preserving the reassurance of light where a person actually walks. The same sensors that dim a lane can also count footsteps and feed a town's planning data.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this requires a city to choose between darkness and security. It asks instead for light that is intentional: dimmed in the small hours, warmed in its colour, and aimed at the ground rather than the sky. A dark sky is not a backward luxury but a measurable sign of a place that has learned to use light with restraint.

sections.label: Passage 3
sections.title: The mathematics of friendship
sections.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 21–30.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Sociologists have long noticed a curious pattern in personal networks. The people we know can be sorted into layers: a handful we are closest to, a wider circle we are fond of, and a still larger band of acquaintances we would recognise but rarely see. This structure is remarkably consistent across cultures, suggesting it reflects something about human capacity rather than fashion.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One influential account proposes that each layer demands a predictable multiple of contact time. To keep a friend in the closest layer, the theory holds, a person must invest roughly weekly attention; the next layer, about monthly; the next, annually. The numbers are approximate, but they capture a real constraint: attention is a budget, and every promotion into a closer layer draws from a finite store.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The total size of a person's active network also appears to plateau. Large surveys find that even the most sociable individuals rarely sustain more than about 150 relationships that feel genuinely personal. Beyond that, names blur and obligations thin. This ceiling is sometimes called the limitation of a mind that evolved for smaller ancestral groups.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Technology complicates the picture. Online tools make it trivial to accumulate thousands of weakly tied contacts, yet the inner layers do not expand to match. People report feeling more connected and, at the same time, more stretched. The instruments of connection have outrun the psychology of connection, leaving a gap between the size of a list and the depth of a bond.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is a practical lesson here for organisations. Teams that grow past a certain size begin to fragment into subgroups that no longer share context. The pattern is not a failure of morale but a predictable effect of how many relationships any member can hold at once. Small, overlapping units tend to preserve the trust that larger ones lose.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this reduces friendship to arithmetic. Affection, loyalty and luck still decide who lands in which layer, and the layers shift across a lifetime. What the numbers offer is a gentle reminder that closeness is built from repeated, unglamorous attention, and that no message sent in bulk can substitute for the time a real relationship requires.

sections.label: Passage 4
sections.title: Urban mining: reclaiming the city's hidden materials
sections.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 31–40.

passage.title: Urban mining: reclaiming the city's hidden materials

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every building, phone and discarded laptop is a concentrated store of metals that someone once dug from the earth. The practice of recovering those materials from the built environment, rather than from a mine, is called urban mining. Its appeal is simple: the concentration of copper, gold and rare elements in electronic waste can exceed that in natural ore, and the material is already above ground, sorted by accident of ownership.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The logic is partly environmental. Conventional mining scars landscapes, consumes vast amounts of water, and produces waste that must be contained for generations. Recovering metal from old equipment avoids some of that harm, provided the recovery itself is clean. The catch is that crude recycling often trades one pollution problem for another when it is done without controls.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Economics decides what gets recovered. When the price of a metal is high, collection and refining become worthwhile; when it falls, the same material is dumped. This volatility means the industry lurches between boom and neglect, and valuable resources are lost in the quiet years. A steadier policy signal, such as a levy on landfilling, can smooth the cycle.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Design is the quieter lever. Equipment that is glued, sealed and mixed together is expensive to take apart, so its materials are rarely reclaimed. Products built to be opened, identified and separated flip the economics before a single item reaches a recycling plant. The cheapest gram of recovered metal is the one a manufacturer made easy to remove.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There are limits. Not every city has the infrastructure, and informal collectors who do much of the world's recycling often work in hazardous conditions for little pay. A just urban-mining system has to protect those workers and capture the material they already handle, rather than displace them. Efficiency and fairness pull in the same direction only when both are designed for.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Urban mining will not replace conventional extraction, and it should not be sold as a complete answer to resource demand. What it offers is a different habit: treating the city as a stockpile to be tended, where yesterday's device becomes tomorrow's supply. That shift in perspective may matter as much as any tonne of metal recovered.
